Per-capability adaptation time dropped from days to hours (descriptive records, not controlled measurements).
AI.conclusion: Initial evidence for cross-embodiment knowledge exchange is demonstrated; fleet-level autonomous evolution and controlled with/without-packet comparisons remain future work.

title: SMART: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Articulated Object Manipulation via Large-Scale Synthetic Pretraining
summary: The ability to interact with articulated objects is essential for embodied intelligent systems, but collecting large-scale real-world demonstrations for these interactions remains challenging due to the precise contact and constraint-following motions involved. Although simulation provides a promising alternative, existing synthetic data efforts cover limited articulated-object categories, while general-purpose synthesis pipelines lack explicit designs for part-level semantics and articulation constraints, hindering agentic task generation and scalable synthesis of high-quality articulated-manipulation demonstrations. To bridge this gap, we introduce SMART, a scalable system leveraging large-scale Synthesized Manipulation demonstrations for ARTiculated-object manipulation. At its core, we develop SMART-Sim, a simulation platform with articulation-aware design that enables effective task generation and efficient demonstration collection. Building on SMART-Sim, we apply agentic task generation and design a scalable distributed synthesis system, using them to synthesize SMART-Data, comprising over 1M demonstrations across 44 atomic task types, 5 robot setups, and 2,507 articulated objects. The vision-language-action (VLA) model pretrained on SMART-Data shows competitive performance on simulation benchmarks and achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and scalable performance in real-world articulated-object manipulation tasks. This highlights the potential of synthetic demonstrations in providing effective and scalable supervision for improving VLA model performance in contact-rich articulated-object manipulation.

AI.tldr: SMART is a scalable system for generating synthetic manipulation demonstrations for articulated objects, using SMART-Sim (an articulation-aware simulation platform) and agentic task generation to produce over 1M demonstrations across 44 task types, 5 robot setups, and 2,507 objects, enabling VLA models to achieve competitive performance and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in contact-rich manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Interacting with articulated objects is essential for embodied intelligent systems, but collecting large-scale real-world demonstrations is challenging due to precise contact and constraint-following motions. Existing synthetic data efforts are limited in coverage of articulated-object categories, while general-purpose synthesis pipelines lack explicit designs for part-level semantics and articulation constraints, hindering agentic task generation and scalable synthesis of high-quality demonstrations.
AI.method: The researchers introduce SMART, a scalable system leveraging large-scale Synthesized Manipulation demonstrations for ARTiculated-object manipulation. At its core, they develop SMART-Sim, a simulation platform with articulation-aware design that enables effective task generation and efficient demonstration collection. Building on SMART-Sim, they apply agentic task generation and design a scalable distributed synthesis system to synthesize SMART-Data.
AI.result: SMART-Data comprises over 1M demonstrations across 44 atomic task types, 5 robot setups, and 2,507 articulated objects. A vision-language-action (VLA) model pretrained on SMART-Data demonstrates competitive performance on simulation benchmarks and achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with scalable performance in real-world articulated-object manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic demonstrations provide effective and scalable supervision for improving VLA model performance in contact-rich articulated-object manipulation, highlighting the potential of synthetic data to bridge the gap between simulation and real-world robotics applications.

title: EigenDEXplore: Structured Exploration for Dexterous Manipulation with Human Priors
summary: Dexterous manipulation poses a challenging high-dimensional optimization problem, as useful behaviors require coordinated motion across many hand joints. In reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based trajectory optimization, exploration commonly relies on independent robot joint perturbations, making coordinated behaviors difficult to discover. Prior work reduces this search space for grasp learning using low-dimensional spaces of coordinated joint motions learned from human hand data, but this restricts the expressivity required for general manipulation. Some combine learned and joint-space actions to restore expressivity, but this increases dimensionality and introduces redundancy. We study these effects across diverse manipulation settings, varying action dimensionality, exploration strategy, and the source of human data. Our experiments suggest that human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than change the action representation. Motivated by this finding, we propose EigenDEXplore, which induces correlated exploration by adding perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise, leaving the action space unchanged. Across multiple dexterous hands, EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines in grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation. These gains span unstructured and reference-guided RL, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment, and are largest in settings with less reward shaping and curriculum design.

AI.tldr: EigenDEXplore uses human-motion priors to induce correlated exploration in high-dimensional manipulation tasks by adding perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise, consistently outperforming joint-space and learned action-space baselines across multiple dexterous hands and manipulation settings.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation is a high-dimensional optimization problem where current RL and trajectory optimization methods use independent joint perturbations, making coordinated behaviors difficult to discover. Prior approaches using low-dimensional human motion spaces restrict expressivity, while combining learned and joint-space actions increases dimensionality and redundancy.
AI.method: The authors studied human-motion priors across diverse manipulation settings, varying action dimensionality, exploration strategies, and human data sources. Based on findings that human-motion priors are most effective for structuring exploration rather than changing action representation, they propose EigenDEXplore: a method that adds perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise while keeping the action space unchanged.
AI.result: EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines in grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation across multiple dexterous hands. The gains are largest in settings with less reward shaping and curriculum design, and span unstructured and reference-guided RL, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment.
AI.conclusion: Human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than change the action representation. EigenDEXplore achieves this by inducing correlated exploration through human-derived eigenvectors, demonstrating broad applicability across different learning paradigms and robotic platforms.

title: ExoBridge: Learning a Bare Hand to Hand-Worn Exoskeleton Mapping through Human Limb Coupling
summary: Human video offers a scalable source of experience for dexterous robot learning, but obtaining motion and tactile supervision while preserving bare hand interaction remains challenging. We present ExoBridge, a framework that leverages human limb coupling to learn a bridging function from bare hand video to the motion and tactile state of a sensorized exoskeleton. Our central idea is to use coordinated bimanual behavior to connect an uninstrumented visual source with a measured manipulation interface. During collection, one hand remains bare and provides visual observations, while the opposite hand wears the exoskeleton and supplies synchronized motion and tactile measurements. These paired demonstrations train a temporal visual model to predict fingertip contact, continuous tactile intensity, and relative encoder motion from bare hand video alone. The exoskeleton defines an intermediate state space whose motion coordinates are linked to a dexterous robot hand through existing calibration. Evaluation on 1,215 demonstrations across four manipulation tasks uses held out collection sessions and yields a pooled any contact AUROC of 0.916 and a Pearson correlation of 0.790 for tactile intensity. The learned bridge also predicts relative changes in exoskeleton configuration from bare hand video. These results demonstrate that human limb coupling can turn exoskeleton measurements into supervision for bare hand video, establishing a learned bridge between human visual demonstrations and a robot oriented manipulation interface.

AI.tldr: ExoBridge leverages human limb coupling to learn a mapping from bare hand video to exoskeleton motion and tactile states, enabling scalable dexterous robot learning through synchronized bimanual demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Human video offers scalable experience for dexterous robot learning, but obtaining motion and tactile supervision while preserving bare hand interaction remains challenging.
AI.method: ExoBridge uses coordinated bimanual demonstrations where one hand remains bare (providing visual observations) while the opposite hand wears a sensorized exoskeleton (supplying synchronized motion and tactile measurements). A temporal visual model is trained to predict fingertip contact, continuous tactile intensity, and relative encoder motion from bare hand video alone. The exoskeleton defines an intermediate state space linked to a dexterous robot hand through calibration.
AI.result: Evaluated on 1,215 demonstrations across four manipulation tasks with held-out collection sessions, ExoBridge achieved a pooled any contact AUROC of 0.916 and a Pearson correlation of 0.790 for tactile intensity prediction. The learned bridge also successfully predicts relative changes in exoskeleton configuration from bare hand video.
AI.conclusion: Human limb coupling can effectively turn exoskeleton measurements into supervision for bare hand video, establishing a learned bridge between human visual demonstrations and a robot-oriented manipulation interface, thereby enabling scalable dexterous robot learning.

title: ESP: Energy-Score Policy for One-Step Multimodal Action Generation
summary: Generative action models based on diffusion and flow matching have been increasingly adopted in vision-language-action (VLA) policies for their ability to capture diverse behaviors, including multiple valid action sequences under the same observation and instruction. Their iterative sampling procedures, however, require repeated network evaluations to generate each action chunk, increasing inference latency in closed-loop control. We propose ESP (Energy-Score Policy), a teacher-free approach that maps policy context and noise directly to an action chunk in a single network evaluation. ESP trains the action head with the energy score rather than mean squared error. Whereas squared-error regression targets the conditional mean, the energy score is strictly proper: its expected value is uniquely minimized by the target distribution. This provides a principled objective for learning multimodal action distributions without iterative sampling, with exact recovery at the population optimum when the model can represent the target distribution. Experiments on both simulation and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate competitive task success with substantially lower action-generation latency than the flow matching baseline. These results support direct distributional learning as an efficient alternative to iterative generative robot policies.

AI.tldr: ESP is a teacher-free VLA policy that maps policy context and noise directly to action chunks in a single network evaluation using an energy score objective, achieving competitive task success with substantially lower inference latency than iterative generative models.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and flow matching generative models can capture diverse valid action sequences but require repeated network evaluations for each action chunk, increasing inference latency in closed-loop control.
AI.method: ESP maps policy context and noise directly to an action chunk in a single network evaluation. It trains the action head with the energy score (a strictly proper scoring rule) rather than mean squared error, enabling principled learning of multimodal action distributions without iterative sampling.
AI.result: Experiments on both simulation and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate competitive task success with substantially lower action-generation latency than the flow matching baseline.
AI.conclusion: Direct distributional learning via energy-score policies provides an efficient alternative to iterative generative robot policies, eliminating repeated evaluations while maintaining performance.

title: Seeing Through the Displaced Frame: Privileged Noise Distillation for Vision-Force Precision Assembly
summary: Pose error in precision assembly can corrupt not only what a robot observes but also the coordinate frame in which it acts. On the FORGE benchmark, the official state-based policy succeeds in 97% to 99% of episodes with the true pose but only 32% to 60% at the benchmark's $σ=5$ mm pose-noise setting. The same estimated pose enters the observation and anchors the action frame, making the offset unidentifiable from proprioceptive state alone before contact. We supply this missing information during training in two ways. A privileged teacher observes the offset in simulation, while clean demonstrations can instead be relabelled into the displaced frame in closed form. The deployed student is trained with behaviour cloning followed by one DAgger round and receives only noisy state, a raw wrench window, and two RGB cameras at test time. On the unmodified FORGE tasks, the teacher-route student maintains 92% to 99% success across $σ=0$ to 5 mm, while six non-privileged baselines fall to 2% to 80%. A matched behaviour-cloning experiment isolates the source of this robustness. With the same student architecture, data budget, and training procedure, demonstrations generated without offset access yield only 31.5% success at $σ=5$ mm, whereas privileged and relabelled demonstrations reach 88.7% and 95.8%. Deployed zero-shot on a Franka, the student reaches 83.3% pooled success at $σ=5$ mm against 34.4% for the strongest state-based policy. Deployable sensing alone is insufficient. Robustness requires supervision that encodes compensation for the latent frame offset.Project page: https://drychang.github.io/displaced-frame/

AI.tldr: This paper addresses pose error and frame offset issues in robotic precision assembly by using privileged supervision (teacher demonstrations with offset information) to train a student policy that can generalize to noisy real-world conditions without privileged information at deployment.
AI.motivation: Pose error corrupts both robot observations and action coordinate frames. On the FORGE benchmark, state-based policies fail dramatically under pose noise (only 32-60% success at σ=5mm vs 97-99% with true pose), and the frame offset is unidentifiable from proprioceptive state alone before contact. Deployable sensing alone is insufficient for robustness.
AI.method: Two training approaches: (1) A privileged teacher that observes the frame offset in simulation; (2) Relabeling clean demonstrations into the displaced frame using closed-form transformations. The deployed student receives only noisy state, raw wrench window, and two RGB cameras, trained via behavior cloning followed by one DAgger round.
AI.result: Teacher-route student maintains 92-99% success across σ=0 to 5mm noise levels, while non-privileged baselines achieve only 2-80% success. Matched behavior cloning experiments show: without offset access (31.5% success at σ=5mm), privileged demonstrations (88.7%), and relabeled demonstrations (95.8%). Deployed on Franka, the student achieves 83.3% pooled success at σ=5mm versus 34.4% for the best state-based policy.
AI.conclusion: Robustness requires supervision that encodes compensation for the latent frame offset. Deployable sensing alone is insufficient; privileged information during training enables the student to generalize robustly to noisy real-world conditions without requiring that information at deployment time.

title: CoRE: Learning Collaboration-Role Experts for Decentralized Collaborative Manipulation with One Policy
summary: Collaborative manipulation requires robots to perform complementary actions as interactions unfold. We study single-policy decentralized collaboration: every robot runs the same policy from its visual observations and proprioception, without task prompts, identity labels, or inter-robot messages. The challenge is to learn complementary team behaviors within shared parameters and select appropriate actions from each robot's local observations. We introduce CoRE, which learns Collaboration-Role Experts from pooled multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations. Fused appearance and geometry provide local interaction evidence. Query-conditioned cross-attention experts provide adaptable prediction paths, which a local router combines at each action-chunk position. During training, an action-expert alignment loss supervises expert selection using relative forced-route prediction errors against demonstrations under fixed inputs, without role labels. Across simulation benchmarks, CoRE achieves the highest average performance among evaluated decentralized methods. Physical experiments demonstrate effective collaboration across diverse manipulation tasks and robustness to partner delays and slowdowns. Project page: https://aus.bot/research/core/.

AI.tldr: CoRE learns single-policy decentralized collaboration by training Collaboration-Role Experts from pooled multi-robot demonstrations using query-conditioned cross-attention and an action-expert alignment loss for role selection without explicit labels.
AI.motivation: Collaborative manipulation requires robots to perform complementary actions. The challenge is learning complementary team behaviors within shared parameters and selecting appropriate actions from local observations without task prompts, identity labels, or inter-robot messages.
AI.method: CoRE learns Collaboration-Role Experts from pooled multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations. It uses fused appearance and geometry for local interaction evidence, query-conditioned cross-attention experts for adaptable prediction paths, and a local router to combine them at each action-chunk position. An action-expert alignment loss supervises expert selection using relative forced-route prediction errors against demonstrations without role labels.
AI.result: Across simulation benchmarks, CoRE achieves the highest average performance among evaluated decentralized methods. Physical experiments demonstrate effective collaboration across diverse manipulation tasks and robustness to partner delays and slowdowns.
AI.conclusion: CoRE enables effective decentralized collaboration in robotics without explicit communication or role labels, using a single shared policy that learns appropriate role behaviors from demonstrations.

title: StairVLA: Stage-Aware Hierarchical Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly rely on diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads to generate continuous robot actions. These action heads typically process the denoising trajectory in a largely uniform manner. However, we observe that the conditioning focus naturally shifts across denoising stages: early stages combine language instructions and visual observations to establish a coarse action trajectory, whereas later stages place greater emphasis on current visual observations for action alignment. Based on this insight, we introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework that uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local refinement. A high-level VLA performs early denoising to produce a reusable long-horizon partially denoised action trajectory, while a lightweight refiner operates at a higher frequency to refine local action chunks using the latest observations. This design amortizes expensive high-level VLA computation while preserving frequent closed-loop correction. On LIBERO, our GR00T-style instantiation improves average success from 96.5% to 97.8% while reducing amortized inference latency from 115.0 ms to 44.2 ms per action chunk. More broadly, across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, StairVLA consistently reduces inference cost while maintaining strong task performance.

AI.tldr: StairVLA introduces a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework for VLA models that separates coarse long-horizon planning (high-level VLA) from local refinement (lightweight refiner), reducing inference cost while maintaining high task performance.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models process denoising trajectories uniformly, but the paper observes that conditioning focus naturally shifts: early stages combine language and visual observations for coarse action trajectories, while later stages emphasize current visual observations for action alignment.
AI.method: StairVLA uses partially denoised actions as an interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local refinement. A high-level VLA performs early denoising to produce reusable partially denoised action trajectories, while a lightweight refiner operates at higher frequency to refine local action chunks using latest observations.
AI.result: On LIBERO (GR00T-style instantiation), StairVLA improves average success from 96.5% to 97.8% and reduces amortized inference latency from 115.0ms to 44.2ms per action chunk. Consistent improvements observed across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: StairVLA consistently reduces inference cost while maintaining strong task performance across diverse settings, demonstrating that amortizing expensive high-level VLA computation through reusable partially denoised trajectories enables efficient closed-loop control.

title: Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization for Constrained Locomotion Planning
summary: Constrained Locomotion Planning (CLP) for quadrupeds and humanoids, where robots must satisfy collision avoidance, contact consistency, kinematic feasibility, and support constraints, is challenging under high-dimensional dynamics and highly non-convex environments. Recent Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) approaches recast trajectory optimization as posterior sampling over trajectories, using known dynamics and Monte Carlo rollouts to analytically estimate the denoising score function without demonstration learning. While constrained variants further incorporate feasibility into model-based score rollouts and show promising performance, they are still limited by (1) lacking a task-modulated active constraint geometry that shapes the score direction and reverse stochasticity, and (2) using deterministic DDPM-style reverse transport without adaptive scheduling across different generative transports. Therefore, we introduce Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization (2GO) for constrained locomotion, which turns active constraint geometry into executable denoising operators through normal- induced metric shaping, tangent-space stochastic filtering, and CFS-based retraction. 2GO further decouples generative transport from reverse stochasticity through an adaptive diffusion and flow-like schedule. Experiments on constrained quadruped and humanoid locomotion demonstrate strong performance in discrete foothold selection and continuous posture planning, with higher success rates, fewer violations, and improved execution compatibility.

AI.tldr: 2GO is a Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization approach that addresses limitations of constrained Model-Based Diffusion methods by incorporating task-modulated active constraint geometry and adaptive diffusion/flow-like scheduling, demonstrating strong performance in constrained quadruped and humanoid locomotion.
AI.motivation: Constrained locomotion planning is challenging due to high-dimensional dynamics and non-convex environments. Existing Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) constrained variants are limited by (1) lacking task-modulated active constraint geometry to shape score direction and reverse stochasticity, and (2) using deterministic DDPM-style reverse transport without adaptive scheduling across different generative transports.
AI.method: 2GO introduces a framework that transforms active constraint geometry into executable denoising operators through three key mechanisms: (1) normal-induced metric shaping, (2) tangent-space stochastic filtering, and (3) CFS-based retraction. Additionally, it decouples generative transport from reverse stochasticity via an adaptive diffusion and flow-like schedule.
AI.result: Experiments on constrained quadruped and humanoid locomotion demonstrate 2GO's strong performance in discrete foothold selection and continuous posture planning, achieving higher success rates, fewer violations, and improved execution compatibility compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: 2GO successfully addresses the limitations of previous constrained MBD methods by incorporating task-modulated active constraint geometry and adaptive scheduling, demonstrating superior performance in constrained locomotion tasks across both quadruped and humanoid robots.

title: Multi-Robot Multi-Goal Motion Planning with Stochastic Skills
summary: As robots are increasingly deployed in groups and share workspaces to execute real-world tasks, planning their concurrent motions around complex manipulation skills becomes essential. These skills involve continuous physical execution and may exhibit stochastic behavior, resulting in variable execution times and uncertain continuous trajectories. Existing planners either limit execution to single-robot scenarios, rely on open-loop paths, or use post-hoc scheduling that prevents dynamic coordination. In this paper, we address this gap by integrating stochastic skills into sampling-based multi-robot planning by formulating the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over a multi-modal composite roadmap. For stochastic skills, solving the MDP yields a reactive policy that allows controllable robots to dynamically adapt their motions in response to other robots' execution of manipulation skills. By resolving skill uncertainty directly at planning time, this approach avoids the pessimism of conservative baselines and unlocks robust, dynamic multi-robot coordination. Code for the planners is available at https://www.vhartmann.com/stochastic-skills.

AI.tldr: A sampling-based multi-robot planner that integrates stochastic manipulation skills via MDP over multi-modal composite roadmaps, enabling reactive dynamic coordination and avoiding conservative baselines.
AI.motivation: Robots increasingly operate in collaborative groups with complex manipulation skills that exhibit stochastic behavior, variable execution times, and uncertain trajectories. Existing multi-robot planners are limited by single-robot scenarios, open-loop paths, or post-hoc scheduling that prevents dynamic coordination.
AI.method: The paper integrates stochastic skills into sampling-based multi-robot planning by formulating the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over a multi-modal composite roadmap. Solving the MDP yields a reactive policy that allows controllable robots to dynamically adapt motions in response to other robots executing manipulation skills.
AI.result: By resolving skill uncertainty directly at planning time, the approach avoids the pessimism of conservative baselines and enables robust, dynamic multi-robot coordination. Code is available at https://www.vhartmann.com/stochastic-skills.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MDP-based planner provides a principled framework for handling stochastic manipulation skills in multi-robot systems, achieving dynamic coordination that surpasses conservative baselines through reactive policy generation at planning time.

title: CUSP: CUSUM-Governed Survival Hazard Alarms at the Perception Onset for Off-Road Navigation
summary: Off-road navigation exposes a robot to potentially hazardous terrain en route. Although learning-based navigation uses safety supervision to choose which path to drive, it provides no runtime alarm when the robot following that path is heading into danger. Such an alarm must be learned from field logs, where human intervention preempts the failure and the failure itself is therefore never observed. The human judges driving unsafe early but typically intervenes only once failure is clearly near, so the intervention marks that judgment late. That earlier judgment is what a runtime alarm must detect, yet no prior intervention-supervised method has targeted it. To address this problem, we introduce CUSP (CUSUM-governed Survival model of the Perception onset), a model-agnostic runtime hazard alarm that learns this moment from intervention-terminated logs. "Cusp" is a word for the point at which one state is about to turn into another, and the moment we target is exactly such a cusp: the point at which safe driving turns unsafe in a human's judgment. We call this point the perception onset and annotate it separately from the intervention. A visual hazard head is trained on the annotated onset with a discrete-time survival objective so that driving with and without an onset both supervise the head, and a CUSUM accumulates the predicted onset risk into alarms. We evaluate CUSP at five unseen sites, two autonomous and three teleoperated, with 142 events and every method tuned to the same rate of ten false alarms per hour. CUSP detected 85 events compared to 26 for the best of nine adapted baselines, and the margin comes from hazards to which every signal in the navigation model is blind.

AI.tldr: CUSP is a model-agnostic runtime hazard alarm for off-road navigation that learns the "perception onset" - the moment when safe driving turns unsafe in a human's judgment - from intervention-terminated logs using a CUSUM-governed survival model.
AI.motivation: Learning-based navigation lacks runtime alarms for hazardous terrain, and existing intervention-supervised methods cannot target the early judgment moment before human intervention. Humans judge driving unsafe early but intervene only near failure, so the critical moment is never observed in field logs.
AI.method: CUSP (CUSUM-governed Survival model of the Perception onset) annotates the "perception onset" (the cusp where safe turns unsafe) separately from intervention. A visual hazard head is trained with discrete-time survival objective supervised by both safe and unsafe driving episodes. A CUSUM accumulates predicted onset risk into alarms.
AI.result: Evaluated at five unseen sites (142 events, ten false alarms/hour). CUSP detected 85 events vs 26 for the best baseline, detecting hazards invisible to the navigation model signals.
AI.conclusion: CUSP effectively learns the critical perception onset moment from human intervention logs, outperforming nine adapted baselines by a significant margin due to detecting hazards that all navigation model signals are blind to.

title: Beyond Retargeting: Low-Latency and Robust Humanoid Whole-Body Teleoperation with Learned Atomic Motion Primitives
summary: Humanoid whole-body teleoperation translates human motion into stable robot behavior in real time. Existing systems typically rely on online motion retargeting to bridge human--robot morphological differences, but this process adds latency and can produce physically infeasible targets. Meanwhile, diverse, noisy, and partial human-motion observations often fall outside the training distribution, potentially causing unstable robot behavior. We propose a retargeting-free policy that maps raw human motion directly to robot joint commands in a single forward pass, eliminating online kinematic adaptation. To improve robustness, we learn a codebook of full-body motion primitives that projects out-of-distribution observations onto plausible motion prototypes and recovers full-body motion from partial inputs. Experiments on a Unitree~G1 in simulation and on hardware, using virtual reality, optical mocap, text-to-motion generation, and monocular video inputs, show that our method outperforms baselines in latency and robustness.

AI.tldr: A retargeting-free policy that maps raw human motion directly to robot joint commands in a single forward pass using a codebook of full-body motion primitives for robustness against noisy and partial inputs.
AI.motivation: Existing whole-body teleoperation systems rely on online motion retargeting which introduces latency and can generate physically infeasible targets. Additionally, diverse, noisy, and partial human-motion observations often fall outside the training distribution, causing unstable robot behavior.
AI.method: The proposed method learns a codebook of full-body motion primitives that projects out-of-distribution observations onto plausible motion prototypes and recovers full-body motion from partial inputs, enabling a retargeting-free policy that maps raw human motion directly to robot joint commands in a single forward pass.
AI.result: Experiments on Unitree G1 in simulation and on hardware using VR, optical mocap, text-to-motion generation, and monocular video inputs demonstrate that the method outperforms baselines in both latency and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The retargeting-free policy with motion primitive codebook provides superior latency performance and robustness against diverse, noisy, and partial human-motion observations compared to traditional online retargeting approaches.

title: From Model to Prototype: Design and Motor-Flap Propulsion Control of a Twin-Wing Metamorphic UAV
summary: This paper presents the design and control strategy for MetaMorpher, a metamorphic Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), capable of both spinning-wing hover and fixed flying-wing cruise flight. Since control of the cruise configuration is comparatively well established in the literature, this paper focuses on control of the MetaMorpher in hover mode, building on the flight dynamics model and conceptual design validated in previous work. The control algorithm is implemented using one of two phase-synchronized strategies: motor propulsion, which pulses motor thrust in synchrony with the vehicle's rotation, or flap propulsion, a novel strategy that pulses the deflection of the wing-mounted elevons. We evaluate both strategies in simulation through different flight experiments. Simulation results confirm the mathematical model and show stable reference tracking, demonstrating flap propulsion as a lightweight, decoupled alternative for hover control. Experimental testing validated the vertical-dynamics propulsion model against the physical prototype, demonstrating very good steady-state agreement across different configurations.

AI.tldr: MetaMorpher is a metamorphic UAV combining spinning-wing hover and fixed flying-wing cruise capabilities. This paper focuses on developing phase-synchronized control strategies for hover mode, comparing motor propulsion and novel flap propulsion approaches.
AI.motivation: While cruise configuration control is well-established, hover control for metamorphic UAVs requires specialized strategies to handle the unique dynamics of spinning-wing flight. The paper aims to develop lightweight, decoupled hover control alternatives to enhance the versatility of MetaMorpher.
AI.method: The research builds on an existing flight dynamics model and conceptual design. Two phase-synchronized control strategies were implemented and evaluated: motor propulsion (pulsing motor thrust in sync with rotation) and flap propulsion (pulsing wing-mounted elevons). Both strategies were tested in simulation and validated experimentally against a physical prototype.
AI.result: Simulation results confirmed the mathematical model and demonstrated stable reference tracking for both strategies, with flap propulsion emerging as a lightweight, decoupled alternative. Experimental testing showed excellent steady-state agreement between the vertical-dynamics propulsion model and the physical prototype across different configurations.
AI.conclusion: Flap propulsion represents a promising lightweight, decoupled control strategy for MetaMorpher hover mode, validated through both simulation and experimental testing. The successful validation of the vertical-dynamics model against the physical prototype confirms the design's accuracy and paves the way for further development of metamorphic UAV control systems.

title: PACE: Stage-Consistent Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation via Progress-Aligned Context for Execution
summary: Demonstration-conditioned policies provide a natural interface for specifying robot behavior, yet long-horizon manipulation remains difficult when visually similar states recur across different stages or when demonstrations and executions proceed at different speeds. We identify the resulting failure mode as stage confusion and introduce Progress-Aligned Context for Execution (PACE), a stateful method that continually reinterprets a complete demonstration according to realized execution progress. PACE compresses the demonstration into ordered multimodal prompt tokens and uses training-only dual-edge attention supervision to expose its latent stage structure. During execution, an episode-local fast-weight memory causally encodes realized action-observation transitions and modulates prompt cross-attention, producing a progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert without test-time stage labels or stage-specific policies. PACE improves success from 88.9% to 94.0% on LIBERO-Gen Goal Chain, from 79.1% to 83.3% on Spatial Combination, and from 33.3% to 73.3% on the two-step Block Routing tasks. Failure analysis further indicates that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory jointly mitigate stage confusion.

AI.tldr: PACE (Progress-Aligned Context for Execution) is a stateful method that addresses stage confusion in demonstration-conditioned policies by continuously reinterpreting demonstrations according to realized execution progress. It uses ordered multimodal prompt tokens with dual-edge attention supervision to expose latent stage structure, and employs episode-local fast-weight memory to causally encode action-observation transitions during execution, producing progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert without test-time stage labels.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon manipulation remains difficult with demonstration-conditioned policies when visually similar states recur across stages or when demonstrations and executions proceed at different speeds. This creates a "stage confusion" failure mode where the policy cannot reliably distinguish between different stages of a task despite visual similarity.
AI.method: PACE uses three key components: (1) Compression of demonstrations into ordered multimodal prompt tokens; (2) Training-only dual-edge attention supervision to expose latent stage structure; (3) Episode-local fast-weight memory that causally encodes realized action-observation transitions and modulates prompt cross-attention during execution. This produces a progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert without requiring test-time stage labels or stage-specific policies.
AI.result: PACE significantly improves success rates across multiple tasks: LIBERO-Gen Goal Chain (88.9%→94.0%), Spatial Combination (79.1%→83.3%), and two-step Block Routing (33.3%→73.3%). Failure analysis confirms that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory jointly mitigate stage confusion.
AI.conclusion: Stage confusion in long-horizon manipulation can be effectively mitigated by combining structured demonstration alignment (via ordered multimodal prompts and dual-edge attention supervision) with causal execution memory (via fast-weight memory encoding transitions). This approach enables demonstration-conditioned policies to maintain context across variable execution speeds and recurring visually similar states without requiring stage-specific policies or test-time labels.

title: OpenWAM: An Open Framework for Composable World-Action Models
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://openwam.stanford.edu ; Code: https://github.com/OpenWAM/OpenWAM ; Code and project page released June 4, 2026. Equal contribution: Heng Yu, David D. Yuan, Juze Zhang
summary: World-action models (WAMs) couple future prediction with robot control, yet existing systems often vary the video backbone, interaction structure, supervision, and inference procedure simultaneously, making their design choices difficult to compare. We introduce OPENWAM, an open world-action modeling framework built around a common causal robot-video foundation and configurable video-action interaction. Starting from Wan2.2-5B, we perform causal robot-video pretraining on over 10,000 hours of video, then integrate an action expert through a shared Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled generation. OPENWAM achieves high success rates on four LIBERO suites and real-world bimanual tasks; robot-video training with causal adaptation improves VTA success on LIBERO-Long from 68.4% to 97.8%. The same configurable architecture naturally extends to inverse and forward dynamics, allowing us to study how counterfactual transitions improve independently trained dynamics models beyond demonstrations alone. When only the video predictor is adapted to a new task, a frozen local-context inverse dynamics model trained on counterfactual data and demonstrations achieves 84.0% mean success across four held-out LIBERO-90 tasks, compared with 47.0% for a full-context inverse model and 21.5% for a local-context model trained only on demonstrations. For forward dynamics, counterfactual supervision reduces RGB prediction error by 34.5% and raises outcome identification from 21.1% to 71.3% among 16 same-state outcomes. OPENWAM provides a common testbed for comparing WAM interaction designs and for studying dynamics learning from video data beyond successful demonstrations.

AI.tldr: OPENWAM introduces a unified, configurable framework for world-action modeling (WAMs) that uses a shared causal robot-video foundation with a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture supporting multiple interaction modes (joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, decoupled), enabling fair comparison of WAM designs and demonstrating significant improvements from counterfactual supervision in both inverse and forward dynamics learning.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models vary video backbones, interaction structures, supervision, and inference procedures simultaneously, making design choices difficult to compare. There's a need for a common testbed to evaluate and compare WAM architectures.
AI.method: Starting from Wan2.2-5B, OPENWAM performs causal robot-video pretraining on 10,000+ hours of video. It integrates an action expert via a shared Mixture-of-Transformers architecture supporting four interaction modes: joint generation, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled generation. The framework naturally extends to inverse and forward dynamics modeling.
AI.result: Causal adaptation improved VTA success on LIBERO-Long from 68.4% to 97.8%. For inverse dynamics, a frozen local-context model trained on counterfactual data plus demonstrations achieved 84.0% success vs 47.0% for full-context and 21.5% for local-context on demonstrations only. For forward dynamics, counterfactual supervision reduced RGB prediction error by 34.5% and raised outcome identification from 21.1% to 71.3% across 16 same-state outcomes.
AI.conclusion: OPENWAM provides a standardized testbed for comparing WAM interaction designs and for studying dynamics learning from video data beyond successful demonstrations, with counterfactual supervision significantly enhancing both inverse and forward dynamics performance.

title: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Models to Unknown Visual Disruptions During Execution
summary: Visual disruptions can arise while a robot is executing a task, leaving a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to respond without knowing the disruption type or timing. We introduce Self-supervised Adaptation from Leftover Trajectories (SALT), which uses the leftover trajectory, the unexecuted part of the previous action chunk, as self-supervision for test-time adaptation. Because consecutive chunks overlap in time, the leftover provides a temporally aligned target for the current prediction over the same future control interval. At the onset of a visual shift, the leftover can retain a plan formed before the corruption, so updating the policy toward it anchors the adaptation across the shift (Transition Anchoring). SALT keeps the adapted policy and regenerates the current chunk, whose leftover becomes the target at the next replan, carrying the correction forward along the execution trajectory (Sequential Correction Propagation). Supervision comes entirely from the policy's own predictions, requiring no disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations, and a lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories decides when updates begin. On LIBERO-10, SALT increases average success across five persistent visual corruptions from 43.9% to 53.2% with SmolVLA and from 58.7% to 66.0% with GR00T N1.7, while largely preserving nominal performance. On a real robot, it raises task progress averaged over digital and physical disruptions from 0.49 to 0.61.

AI.tldr: SALT is a self-supervised test-time adaptation method for VLA policies that uses leftover trajectories as supervision when visual disruptions occur during robot task execution. It employs Transition Anchoring and Sequential Correction Propagation to adapt policies without needing disruption annotations or expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Visual disruptions can occur during robot task execution, leaving VLA (vision-language-action) policies to respond without knowing the disruption type or timing. Existing adaptation methods often require disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain.
AI.method: SALT uses leftover trajectories (the unexecuted portion of previous action chunks) as self-supervision for test-time adaptation. Key mechanisms: 1) Transition Anchoring - when a visual shift occurs, the leftover retains a plan formed before corruption, anchoring adaptation; 2) Sequential Correction Propagation - the adapted policy regenerates the current chunk, whose leftover becomes the target at the next replan. A lightweight adaptation gate, calibrated only on nominal trajectories, decides when updates begin.
AI.result: On LIBERO-10 benchmark, SALT increased average success across five persistent visual corruptions from 43.9% to 53.2% with SmolVLA and from 58.7% to 66.0% with GR00T N1.7, while preserving nominal performance. On a real robot, it increased task progress from 0.49 to 0.61.
AI.conclusion: SALT achieves robust test-time adaptation for VLA policies using only self-supervision from leftover trajectories, without requiring disruption annotations or target-domain demonstrations. The method maintains performance on nominal trajectories while significantly improving robustness to visual disruptions.

title: Commit While Futures Agree: Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking for Robot Manipulation
summary: Action-chunking policies predict multi-step control sequences, but a fundamental question remains: how much of a predicted action chunk should be committed before replanning? Existing systems typically execute a fixed-length prefix, implicitly assuming that the same execution horizon remains trustworthy across states. Some adaptive methods estimate this horizon from the similarity or stability of predicted actions. However, different actions may lead to the same successful outcome, whereas similar actions can produce different futures, suggesting that commitment should be determined by agreement among imagined futures rather than by similarity in action space. To this end, we propose Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking (CA$^3$C), an inference-time framework built on a simple principle: commit while imagined futures agree, and replan when they diverge. Without modifying or retraining the base policy, CA$^3$C uses an action-conditioned world model to imagine the future consequences of multiple candidate action chunks under the same sampling noise. Using these imagined consequences, we formulate execution-horizon estimation as a Bayesian change-point inference problem and select the execution candidate through future consensus. Across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks, CA$^3$C consistently improves diverse action-chunking policies, achieving up to a 71.8% relative reduction in failure rate over the corresponding base policies.

AI.tldr: CA³C proposes determining action-chunk commitment based on consensus among imagined futures rather than action similarity, using Bayesian change-point inference to decide when to replan without modifying the base policy.
AI.motivation: Existing action-chunking systems either use fixed-length prefixes or estimate execution horizons from action similarity, but similar actions can produce different futures while different actions can lead to the same outcome, suggesting commitment should be based on future consequences rather than action space similarity.
AI.method: Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking (CA³C) uses an action-conditioned world model to imagine futures of multiple candidate action chunks under the same sampling noise, formulates execution-horizon estimation as Bayesian change-point inference, and selects the execution candidate through future consensus—commit while imagined futures agree, replan when they diverge.
AI.result: Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks, CA³C consistently improves diverse action-chunking policies, achieving up to a 71.8% relative reduction in failure rate over base policies without requiring modification or retraining of the base policy.
AI.conclusion: Future consensus among imagined outcomes is a superior metric for determining execution horizons compared to action similarity, and the CA³C framework achieves significant performance gains without requiring base policy modification or retraining.

title: IronMan: Information-Constrained Video-Action Learning for Robot Manipulation
summary: Video Action Models (VAMs) couple visual dynamics modeling with action generation for robot manipulation. However, video representations are not naturally suited to action generation, as exposing the action policy to excessive visual detail can impair its generalization ability. Therefore, we introduce IronMan (Information-constRained videO-actioN learning for robot MANipulation), a robust video-action learning framework built on the information bottleneck principle. The core principle of this framework is to impose information constraints that suppress irrelevant visual information while preserving action-relevant dynamics cues. IronMan employs a dynamics-aware bottleneck that distills noisy, entangled one-step video features into compact world representations. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate strong in-distribution (ID) performance and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness while maintaining efficient inference. IronMan achieves success rates of 99.0% on LIBERO and 79.4% on RoboTwin clean2clean, outperforming all the evaluated baselines. Under OOD shifts, IronMan achieves a success rate of 79.1% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10.4 percentage points. Project page: https://youngsoul0731.github.io/ironman-project-page/

AI.tldr: IronMan is an information-constrained video-action learning framework for robot manipulation that uses a dynamics-aware bottleneck to suppress irrelevant visual information while preserving action-relevant dynamics, achieving strong in-distribution performance (99.0% on LIBERO) and OOD robustness (79.1% on LIBERO-Plus).
AI.motivation: Video representations are not naturally suited to action generation; exposing action policy to excessive visual detail impairs generalization ability, requiring a framework that can selectively filter information while preserving action-relevant dynamics cues.
AI.method: Built on the information bottleneck principle, IronMan employs a dynamics-aware bottleneck that distills noisy, entangled one-step video features into compact world representations by imposing information constraints that suppress irrelevant visual information while preserving action-relevant dynamics cues.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate strong in-distribution performance (99.0% on LIBERO, 79.4% on RoboTwin clean2clean) and OOD robustness (79.1% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding strongest baseline by 10.4 percentage points), outperforming all evaluated baselines while maintaining efficient inference.
AI.conclusion: IronMan successfully achieves robust video-action learning for robot manipulation by effectively balancing information compression with action-relevant feature preservation, demonstrating superior performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios.

title: Reactive Task-Oriented Robot-Human Handovers via Generative Hypothesis Selection
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
summary: When humans hand each other objects, they incorporate both geometric and semantic information into this process. For example, passing a knife with the handle towards the recipient, rather than the blade, is both more ergonomic and safer. Recent state-of-the-art methods for task-oriented robot-human handovers have progressed from modeling object geometry to incorporating object affordances. However, they often forgo predicting the explicit, task-specific hand poses a human selects to utilize an object. Since many objects support multiple interaction modalities, e.g., a claw hammer used to strike or pull nails, this variability must be modeled to achieve robust task-oriented handovers. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach, GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS), which leverages VLM image generation to produce a variety of task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These hypotheses are matched in real time to the observed human hand pose, enabling inference of the most suitable handover configuration. By leveraging VLMs as priors of plausible hand-object interactions, the method produces task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs. We evaluate the standalone interaction proposal module before deploying the full system on a mobile manipulator. In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived our method to have better task understanding than the previous state of the art.

AI.tldr: GENESIS-Handover uses VLM image generation to produce task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses, which are matched to observed human hand poses for robust robot-human handovers, achieving 83.3% better task understanding perception in user studies.
AI.motivation: Humans incorporate both geometric and semantic information when handing objects (e.g., passing a knife handle-first for ergonomics and safety). Previous robot handover methods focused on object affordances but often omitted predicting explicit, task-specific hand poses. Since objects support multiple interaction modalities (e.g., a claw hammer used for striking or pulling nails), modeling this variability is essential for robust task-oriented handovers.
AI.method: GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS) leverages VLM image generation to create diverse task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These hypotheses are matched in real-time to observed human hand poses to infer the most suitable handover configuration. The method uses VLMs as priors for plausible hand-object interactions and produces task-conditioned strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs.
AI.result: In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% of participants perceived the proposed method as having better task understanding than the previous state-of-the-art. The standalone interaction proposal module was evaluated before full system deployment on a mobile manipulator.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging VLMs as priors for plausible hand-object interactions, GENESIS-Handover successfully produces task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs, demonstrating superior task understanding in human evaluations.

title: Vector Map Quality Metrics for Contextual Autonomous Driving Systems
summary: Ensuring safety in autonomous driving requires continuous map maintenance supported by reliable quality indicators. In this context, it is crucial to identify when and where map updates should be triggered, for instance through crowdsourced data, and under which conditions a new map compilation should be deployed. This paper focuses on effective metrics for assessing the quality of vector maps and guiding such decisions. We present a new metric called GOSPAM designed to measure map discrepancies in terms of location errors, existence, and completeness. Through detailed simulations on both point and polyline feature maps, we analyze its sensitivity to common map degradation such as bias, false positives, false negatives, and coordinate errors. The results demonstrate that GOSPAM offers a unified and interpretable measure that effectively captures various forms of map deviation, making it a strong candidate for map quality assessment in automotive applications.

AI.tldr: A new metric called GOSPAM is proposed to measure map discrepancies in terms of location errors, existence, and completeness, enabling effective assessment of vector map quality for autonomous driving applications.
AI.motivation: Ensuring safety in autonomous driving requires continuous map maintenance with reliable quality indicators to identify when and where map updates should be triggered through crowdsourced data and under what conditions a new map compilation should be deployed.
AI.method: The paper presents GOSPAM, a metric that measures map discrepancies in location errors, existence, and completeness. Through detailed simulations on point and polyline feature maps, the sensitivity of GOSPAM to common map degradation factors (bias, false positives, false negatives, and coordinate errors) is analyzed.
AI.result: GOSPAM demonstrates effectiveness as a unified and interpretable measure that captures various forms of map deviation, making it a strong candidate for map quality assessment in automotive applications.
AI.conclusion: GOSPAM provides an effective solution for map quality assessment in autonomous driving, enabling more reliable map maintenance and update decision-making.

title: Navigation with RF Cues: Embodied Perception Action under Multipath Uncertainty
summary: Smart factory inspection requires robots to reach connected equipment without a prior map or known target coordinates. Radio frequency (RF) signals from the target can provide directional cues to complement visual observations when occlusion or poor lighting limits target detection. However, multipath propagation can distort these cues, making it difficult to infer the target's true direction from instantaneous RF measurements. To enable navigation research under these conditions, we first construct a Habitat Sionna RT benchmark that uses detailed scene geometry and assigned material properties to generate aligned visual and RF observations in response to robot actions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an uncertainty aware multimodal navigation framework that jointly estimates target direction and its uncertainty from a history of RF, visual, and pose observations. These estimates inform action selection alongside visual context. Experiments in unseen scenes show relative improvements of 18.2% in success rate (SR) and 11.5% in success weighted by path length (SPL) over the strongest evaluated baseline.

AI.tldr: A multimodal navigation framework combining visual and RF signals with uncertainty awareness for smart factory inspection, achieving 18.2% higher success rate and 11.5% better path efficiency over baselines.
AI.motivation: Smart factory robots need to locate connected equipment without prior maps; visual observations are limited by occlusion or poor lighting, while RF signals provide directional cues but are distorted by multipath propagation, requiring navigation research under these challenging conditions.
AI.method: 1) Constructs Habitat Sionna RT benchmark with detailed scene geometry and material properties to generate aligned visual and RF observations; 2) Proposes uncertainty-aware multimodal navigation framework that jointly estimates target direction and uncertainty from RF, visual, and pose observation history; 3) Uses estimates to inform action selection alongside visual context.
AI.result: In unseen scenes, the proposed framework achieves relative improvements of 18.2% in success rate (SR) and 11.5% in success weighted by path length (SPL) compared to the strongest evaluated baseline.
AI.conclusion: The uncertainty-aware multimodal navigation framework effectively addresses RF signal distortion challenges and significantly outperforms baselines, demonstrating the value of combining visual and RF observations with uncertainty estimation for navigation in smart factory environments.

title: Reactive Exploration of Unknown Environments for Redundant Robots using Virtual Model Control
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures, This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: The exploration of confined, occluded, and partially known spaces poses significant challenges in robotic manipulation. The overall pose of the robotic arm must be carefully controlled to respect tight geometric constraints while avoiding newly discovered obstacles. We address this problem by proposing an active exploration approach for redundant robotic arms with an eye-in-hand camera configuration. Our approach navigates and acquires information in real-time based on a novel scoring method that directly selects a target voxel from the unexplored space using the robot's current state and expected information gain. To move the robot safely toward the target voxel, we utilize Virtual Model Control, which guarantees compliance and enables whole-body reactive obstacle avoidance without the need for path replanning. Simulated and real-robot experiments in both confined and open environments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving over $90\%$ mapping coverage across all tested environments in under $120$ seconds without colliding with obstacles.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an active exploration approach for redundant robotic arms with an eye-in-hand camera to navigate and acquire information in real-time in confined, occluded, and partially known spaces using a novel voxel selection scoring method and Virtual Model Control for safe obstacle avoidance.
AI.motivation: The exploration of confined, occluded, and partially known spaces poses significant challenges in robotic manipulation. The overall pose of the robotic arm must be carefully controlled to respect tight geometric constraints while avoiding newly discovered obstacles.
AI.method: The approach uses a novel scoring method that directly selects a target voxel from the unexplored space using the robot's current state and expected information gain. To move the robot safely toward the target voxel, Virtual Model Control is utilized, which guarantees compliance and enables whole-body reactive obstacle avoidance without the need for path replanning.

AI.conclusion: The proposed active exploration approach with Virtual Model Control effectively addresses the challenges of navigating and acquiring information in real-time for redundant robotic arms with an eye-in-hand camera configuration in confined, occluded, and partially known spaces.

title: Energy-Aware Path Following: Comparative Analysis of Reinforcement Learning and NMPC for Electric Vehicles
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, currently submitted for review at the journal (Robotics and Autonomous Systems) https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/robotics-and-autonomous-systems
summary: Path-following control strategies typically follow the bi-objective optimization dilemma: minimizing deviations from a reference path while maintaining smooth speed profiles. The latter objective is especially relevant for Electric Vehicles (EVs), since their limited driving range can be extended by recovering energy through regenerative braking, a feature that has not yet been sufficiently studied in the literature. In this work, we perform a comparative analysis of four controllers under one common Frenet frame-based kinematic vehicle model, utilizing a validated energy model (VT-CPEM) with explicit regenerative braking. Herein, we implement the following controllers: Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), gain-scheduled Ackermann state-feedback baseline (PID-SF), and a Stanley geometric baseline. To satisfy real-time requirements, we implement the NMPC using JIT-compiled CasADi. Moreover, we train the PPO using traditional straight and S-curve tracks, after which we successfully transfer the unmodified policy to unseen tracks, including: an ISO 3888-1 lane-change, a chicane, randomly-generated parameterized-splines, and a $\pm3^\circ$ graded road. In addition, the policy transfers to a dynamic single-track vehicle model with linear tires, zero-shot with an acceptable initial performance, which was optimized after brief fine-tuning. Thereby, we demonstrate that our PPO is readily transferable to more comprehensive vehicle models. We conclude with a performance analysis of developed controllers and discuss ideas for future work.

AI.method: The study employs a Frenet frame-based kinematic vehicle model combined with a validated VT-CPEM energy model featuring explicit regenerative braking. title: AutodidactWAM: Cross-Modal Self-Distillation from Generated Video to Robot Actions
summary: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos 3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune to a previously unseen robot, a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video-action asymmetry: the video renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We evaluate closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place. The native action succeeds only approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% of the time, respectively, and performs worse on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM, a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, that runs on the model's generated video to recover action estimates. Paired with the native prediction, these recovered actions provide preferred targets for fine-tuning only the action-related layers, while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare supervised relabeling with a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action gate reaches approximately 75%, 47%, and 42% pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success, compared with 17%, 10%, and 7% for the native action. A hybrid objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) performs best: on Oreo, the training object, it reaches 90% pre-grasp and 20% full-task success; on a held-out object, it reaches 80% and 30%. Plain Flow-DPO reaches 0% success despite 1.000 validation preference accuracy, indicating that the combination of training objectives, rather than the contrastive objective alone, drives the observed gains.

This approach achieves 75%/47%/42% pre-grasp/grasp/pick-and-place success on the native model and 90%/20% and 80%/30% on training/held-out objects, significantly outperforming the native action (17%/10%/7%).

title: iGPC: Generative Motion Priors for Object-Aware Humanoid Interaction
summary: Humanoid robots operating in unstructured environments must combine robust whole-body control with the ability to perceive and physically interact with surrounding objects. While large-scale human motion data provides powerful priors for natural and versatile humanoid control, effectively transferring such priors to perception-driven object interaction remains challenging. To address this bottleneck, we propose a framework that extends the recently proposed Generative Pretrained Controller (GPC) from general human motion to full-body humanoid-environment interaction. First, we adapt GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance cues and privileged state information. These experts leverage the pretrained human motion prior while learning task-specific contact behaviors, including reaching toward objects, grasping environmental supports for stabilization, and pushing movable objects. Second, we introduce a perception-driven student that retains the pretrained GPC policy and distills interaction skills from the experts using onboard sensory observations. To bridge the gap between privileged expert observations and sensory inputs, we propose two complementary training objectives that enable effective adaptation of the pretrained motion prior during distillation. Notably, our experiments across multiple whole-body interaction tasks demonstrate that large-scale generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for learning deployable policies for humanoid interactions in contact-rich real-world environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework that extends the Generative Pretrained Controller (GPC) from general human motion to full-body humanoid-environment interaction. By creating perception-driven student models that distill interaction skills from privileged expert controllers conditioned on scene affordance cues, the approach enables humanoid robots to leverage large-scale human motion priors for robust contact-rich interaction in unstructured environments.

While large-scale human motion data provides powerful priors for versatile humanoid control, effectively transferring such priors to perception-driven object interaction remains a significant challenge.
AI.method: The framework extends GPC through two main components: (1) Interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance cues and privileged state information, which learn task-specific contact behaviors like reaching, grasping, and pushing; (2) A perception-driven student that retains the pretrained GPC policy and distills skills from experts using onboard sensory observations, with two complementary training objectives bridging the gap between privileged and sensory observations.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple whole-body interaction tasks demonstrate that large-scale generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for learning deployable policies for humanoid interactions in contact-rich real-world environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully enables humanoid robots to leverage human motion priors for perception-driven interaction in unstructured environments, demonstrating that pretrained motion models can serve as effective foundations for contact-rich real-world interaction policies.

title: Beyond Waypoint Regression: Query-Based Cost Learning over Reachable Ego Futures for End-to-End Driving
comment: Accepted in the 18th Asian Conference on Computer Vision (ACCV 2026)
summary: End-to-end planners based on waypoint regression achieve strong open-loop accuracy, but they primarily learn to mimic expert geometry and remain difficult to adapt to deployment-time safety constraints. We propose a query-based cost-learning framework that estimates bounded costs for dynamically reachable ego trajectory queries, rather than dense BEV cells or a small regressed trajectory set. Compact joint scene tokens capture coherent multimodal agent futures, while contingency-aware cost aggregation and cost-guided intra-cluster MPPI mixing convert the learned cost topology into feasible ego plans. On nuScenes, our method improves over prior cost-estimation planners such as ST-P3 and NMP, outperforms most regression baselines in collision rate, while remaining competitive in L2, and retaining an interpretable cost interface. On real-world driving logs, the proposed planner reduces collision rates compared with SparseDrive and Alpamayo without fine-tuning, while maintaining a diverse set of candidate trajectories.

AI.motivation: End-to-end waypoint regression planners achieve strong open-loop accuracy but primarily mimic expert geometry and struggle to adapt to deployment-time safety constraints.
AI.method: The framework uses query-based cost-learning for dynamically reachable ego trajectory queries (instead of dense BEV cells or small regressed trajectory sets), compact joint scene tokens to capture coherent multimodal agent futures, contingency-aware cost aggregation, and cost-guided intra-cluster MPPI mixing to convert learned cost topology into feasible ego plans.

AI.conclusion: The proposed planner effectively balances safety (collision reduction) with performance (L2 metrics) and maintains interpretability by using a query-based cost-learning approach that estimates bounded costs rather than dense representations.

title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code is available at https://github.com/du-owen/VLA-ACL.

AI.tldr: VLA-ACL learns an action-consistency-based visual token pruning policy that keeps the base VLA model frozen, achieving up to 87.5% token reduction, 75% computation savings, and 1.5x inference speedup while maintaining competitive performance.

Existing pruning approaches are limited: they either rely on indirect training-free heuristics (attention scores, motion thresholds) that may not effectively capture token importance, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model, which limits practical deployment.

The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher model, using ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This approach directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output, enabling principled pruning without modifying the base model.
